guides.title: How to taste wine in four steps
guides.subtitle: Look, swirl, smell, sip. A minute of attention tells you most of what the label won't.

sections.plain: Colour hints at age and grape
sections.detail: Tilt the glass over something white. Reds lose colour and turn brick at the rim as they age; whites deepen from pale lemon towards gold. A pale ruby red is usually a lighter grape such as Pinot Noir; an inky one is more likely Syrah or Cabernet.
examples: Brick or orange rim: an older red
Deep gold white: age, oak or a sweet style

sections.plain: Swirling lifts the aromas to your nose
sections.detail: Swirl for a few seconds, then take short sniffs. Most of what we call flavour is smell. Name the broad family first (fruit, flowers, spice, earth, oak) before hunting for anything precise.
examples: Fruit: red berries, black fruit, citrus, stone fruit

sections.plain: Hold it in your mouth for a few seconds
sections.detail: Let the wine cover your tongue. Notice sweetness on the tip, acidity making your mouth water, tannin drying your gums, and how heavy it feels (body). Then swallow and count how long the flavour lasts: that's the finish.
examples: Flavour lasting 10+ seconds: a long finish, often a sign of quality

questions.q: A red wine that has turned brick-orange at the rim is most likely…
questions.fact: Reds lose their purple colour and turn brick at the rim as they age.

questions.q: Which sensation tells you a wine has high acidity?
questions.fact: Acidity makes you salivate; tannin is the drying one.

questions.q: The "finish" is…
opts: How long the flavour lasts after you swallow
The last glass in the bottle
questions.fact: A long finish is one of the clearest signs of a well-made wine.

tryIt.label: Scan your next bottle and try Blind Call

guides.title: Putting what you like into words
guides.subtitle: Four words are enough to describe almost any wine you enjoy, and to ask for more of it.

sections.plain: Body, acidity, tannin, sweetness
sections.detail: Flavour words vary from person to person, but structure doesn't. "Medium-bodied, fresh, soft tannins, dry" tells a shop or sommelier far more than "fruity".

sections.plain: Red fruit, black fruit, citrus, orchard fruit, spice, earth
sections.detail: Pick the family, not the exact fruit. "Red fruit and a bit of spice" is useful; arguing about raspberry versus cranberry isn't.

sections.plain: It narrows things down fastest
sections.detail: "Nothing too oaky" or "not too dry" rules out whole styles at once. It's the quickest way to get a good recommendation.

questions.q: Which description is most useful to a sommelier?
questions.fact: Structure words mean the same thing to everyone.

questions.q: "Off-dry" means…
questions.fact: Off-dry wines have a touch of sweetness you can just notice.

questions.q: Saying "nothing too oaky" helps because…
opts: It rules out whole styles at once
questions.fact: A dislike narrows the choice faster than a like.

guides.title: Oak, tannin and that creamy feel
guides.subtitle: Three things winemakers choose that change how a wine tastes, and how to spot each one.

sections.plain: From skins, seeds, stems and oak
sections.detail: Red wines ferment with their skins, which is where most tannin comes from. It dries your gums like strong black tea. Thick-skinned grapes such as Cabernet Sauvignon and Nebbiolo are grippy; thin-skinned Pinot Noir and Gamay are silky.
examples: Almost none: most whites and rosés

sections.plain: Barrels add flavour, texture and a little tannin
sections.detail: New oak barrels give vanilla, toast, coconut or spice; old barrels mostly soften the wine without adding flavour. "Unoaked" or "stainless steel" on a label means fresh fruit first.
examples: New French oak: vanilla, toast, subtle spice
American oak: coconut, dill, sweeter vanilla

sections.plain: Why some Chardonnay tastes buttery
sections.detail: A second fermentation turns sharp malic acid (think green apple) into softer lactic acid (think milk). Almost all reds go through it; in whites it's a choice, and it's the source of the buttery note in some Chardonnay.
examples: Reds: nearly all go through it

questions.q: Most of a red wine's tannin comes from…
questions.fact: Reds ferment on their skins, which is where tannin lives.

questions.q: A vanilla or toast note usually comes from…
questions.fact: New oak adds vanilla and toast; older barrels mostly add texture.

questions.q: A buttery Chardonnay has usually been through…
questions.fact: Malolactic fermentation softens sharp acidity and can add a buttery note.

tryIt.label: Scan a bottle and see its oak and tannin

guides.title: Reading a restaurant wine list
guides.subtitle: How lists are laid out, where the value hides and how to choose in under a minute.

sections.plain: By colour, then region or style, then price
sections.detail: Most lists run sparkling, white, rosé, red, sweet. Within each, wines are grouped by country or style and usually rise in price. Glass and carafe options are often on a separate page.
examples: Old World lists: grouped by region
New World lists: often by grape
Short lists: often by style ("light reds")

sections.plain: Lesser-known regions and the second-cheapest trap
sections.detail: Restaurant markups are often highest on famous names people order anyway. Lesser-known regions and grapes tend to give more wine for the money. The second-cheapest bottle isn't automatically the bargain it looks.
examples: Instead of Sancerre: Touraine Sauvignon Blanc
Instead of Chablis Premier Cru: Mâcon-Villages

sections.plain: Start from the food and a price
sections.detail: Decide your price first, pick the colour that suits the food, then choose a style word from your palate ("fresh", "full"). If in doubt, point to a price and describe the style: nobody needs to pronounce anything.
examples: "Around this price, something fresh and white"
"What do you like at this price?"

questions.q: Most wine lists run in which order?
opts: Cheapest to dearest across all wines
questions.fact: Lighter styles usually come first, sweet wines last.

questions.q: Better value on a list is often found in…
opts: The most famous name on the list
questions.fact: Famous names carry the biggest markups because people order them anyway.

questions.q: The easiest way to ask for a bottle without naming it:
opts: Point to a price and describe the style
questions.fact: Pointing to a price keeps the budget private and the recommendation useful.

tryIt.label: Scan a wine list to rank it by your taste

guides.title: Talking to a sommelier
guides.subtitle: They want you to enjoy the wine. Here's what to tell them so you do.

sections.plain: Style, food and budget
sections.detail: Say what you're eating, a wine you've liked, and your budget. That's everything a good sommelier needs, and none of it requires wine vocabulary.
examples: "We're having the lamb and the fish"
Point to a price on the list

sections.plain: Point, don't announce
sections.detail: Pointing at a price on the list tells the sommelier your budget without saying it out loud. A good one will stay at or below it.
examples: Point at a bottle in your range: "something like this"
Ask for a glass to try first

sections.plain: A recommendation is a free lesson
sections.detail: If they suggest a grape or region you don't know, ask why they picked it. You'll learn what links it to what you like, and you can score it in Vinterest afterwards.
examples: "How is it like the Rioja I mentioned?"
Scan the bottle when it arrives

questions.q: What three things help a sommelier most?
opts: Food, a wine you liked and your budget
Your age, the vintage and the cork
The grape, the soil and the oak
questions.fact: Food, a reference wine and a budget are all they need.

questions.q: A discreet way to set a budget is to…
opts: Point at a price on the list
questions.fact: Pointing keeps it private and clear.

questions.q: When a sommelier suggests an unfamiliar wine, a useful question is…
questions.fact: Their reasoning teaches you what links it to your taste.

tryIt.label: Open your sommelier script in WineDNA

guides.title: The bottle arrives: what the tasting is for
guides.subtitle: You're checking the wine is sound, not whether you like it. Here's how, and when to send it back.

sections.plain: Is it the bottle you ordered?
sections.detail: Look at the producer, wine and vintage. A different vintage from the list is common; say so if it matters to you.

sections.plain: The pour is for spotting a fault
sections.detail: A corked wine smells of damp cardboard or a musty cellar and tastes flat. That's a fault, and the restaurant should replace it. Not liking the style isn't a fault.
examples: Oxidised: flat, bruised apple, sherry-like (in a wine that shouldn't be)
Too warm: ask for an ice bucket instead

sections.plain: "I think this might be corked"
sections.detail: Say it plainly and ask them to taste it. Any good restaurant will replace a faulty bottle without fuss.
examples: "Could you taste this? I think it's corked."
"It's a little warm, could we chill it?"

questions.q: The tasting pour at a restaurant is mainly to check…
questions.fact: It's a check for faults, not a chance to change your mind about the style.

questions.q: A corked wine smells of…
opts: Damp cardboard or a musty cellar
questions.fact: Cork taint (TCA) gives a musty, wet-cardboard smell and dulls the fruit.

questions.q: A red served too warm is best fixed by…
opts: A few minutes in an ice bucket
questions.fact: Temperature isn't a fault; a short chill fixes it.

guides.title: What more money actually buys
guides.subtitle: Where the jump in quality is real, and where you're paying for a name.

sections.plain: Tax and costs take most of the price
sections.detail: In many countries a big share of a cheap bottle's price is duty, VAT, glass and transport, so a small step up can double what's spent on the wine itself.
examples: Cheapest shelf: mostly tax and bottle
A step up: noticeably more wine in the price

sections.plain: Where quality rises fastest
sections.detail: Between the entry level and the famous names you'll find the best value: good producers from less famous regions, and second wines of big names.
examples: Côtes du Rhône Villages over plain Côtes du Rhône
Crianza from a good Rioja house

sections.plain: Famous regions cost more for the same quality
sections.detail: Burgundy, Champagne houses and top Napa carry a premium for scarcity and reputation. Your own scores are the best guide to whether it's worth it for you.
examples: Crémant instead of Champagne for everyday bubbles
Beaujolais crus instead of red Burgundy
Your WineDNA Value section shows your own sweet spot

questions.q: Why can a small step up in price buy much better wine at the cheap end?
opts: Fixed costs like tax and glass take most of a cheap bottle's price
Shops lose money on cheap wine
questions.fact: Once fixed costs are covered, extra spend goes into the wine itself.

questions.q: A good-value alternative to Champagne for everyday bubbles is…
questions.fact: Crémant is made the same way as Champagne, usually for much less.

questions.q: The best guide to whether an expensive wine is worth it for you is…
questions.fact: Value is personal: your scores show where spending more has paid off.

tryIt.label: See your Value section in WineDNA

guides.title: Reading the label for quality clues
guides.subtitle: Classification words, the producer and the vintage: what each promises and what it doesn't.

sections.plain: Rules about where and how, not guarantees of taste
sections.detail: AOC, DOCG, DOCa and similar mean the wine followed rules about origin, grapes and sometimes ageing. A more specific place (a village or single vineyard) usually means stricter rules and higher prices.
examples: France: AOC, then village, then Premier and Grand Cru

sections.plain: Reserva and Gran Reserva mean something in Spain
sections.detail: In Rioja, Crianza, Reserva and Gran Reserva are legal minimum ageing times. In many other countries "Reserve" on a label has no legal meaning at all.
examples: Rioja Reserva: at least 3 years, 1 in oak
Rioja Gran Reserva: at least 5 years, 2 in oak
"Reserve" in the USA or Australia: a marketing word

sections.plain: Matters most in marginal climates
sections.detail: The year matters more where weather varies a lot (Bordeaux, Burgundy, Germany) and less where it's reliably warm. For everyday wines, a producer you trust matters more than the year.
examples: Big vintage swings: Bordeaux, Burgundy, Mosel
Steadier: much of Australia, California, Argentina
Non-vintage (NV): a blend of years for a consistent style

questions.q: A classification like AOC or DOCG mainly guarantees…
opts: The wine followed rules on origin and production
questions.fact: Classifications are about rules of origin and method, not taste.

questions.q: In Rioja, "Gran Reserva" means…
opts: At least 5 years of ageing, 2 in oak
questions.fact: Rioja's ageing terms are legal minimums.

questions.q: Vintage matters most in…
opts: Regions with variable weather, like Burgundy
questions.fact: Marginal climates swing the most from year to year.

tryIt.label: Scan a label to see what it says

guides.title: Choosing wine as a gift
guides.subtitle: How to pick something they'll enjoy, even if you don't know their taste.

sections.plain: Buy one step up from what they drink
sections.detail: A better producer or a more specific region of a wine they already love is almost always welcome.
examples: They like Malbec: a Malbec from a named sub-region of Mendoza
They like Prosecco: a Champagne or Crémant
They like Rioja: a Reserva from a classic house

sections.plain: Crowd-pleasing styles
sections.detail: Medium-bodied reds with soft tannins and fresh, dry whites suit most people. Sparkling wine works for almost any occasion.
examples: Red: Côtes du Rhône, Chianti Classico, Pinot Noir

sections.plain: Ask the shop and write a note
sections.detail: A good independent shop will help you choose by budget. A short note on why you picked it ("it's from the region we visited") often means more than the price.
examples: Tell the shop your budget and the occasion
Add a note on when to drink it

questions.q: If you know the person loves a wine, a safe gift is…
opts: A step up in the same style
questions.fact: A better version of what they love is rarely wrong.

questions.q: Which style suits the widest range of people?
questions.fact: Soft, medium-bodied reds are the most widely enjoyed.

questions.q: Sparkling wine is a good default gift because…
questions.fact: Bubbles feel like a celebration whatever the occasion.

tryIt.label: Scan the shelf before you buy

guides.title: Four pairing rules that actually work
guides.subtitle: Forget the rulebook. These four cover most meals.

sections.plain: Fresh wines cut through rich food
sections.detail: High-acid wines refresh your mouth between bites of fatty or salty food, the way a squeeze of lemon does.

sections.plain: Grippy reds with red meat
sections.detail: Protein and fat soften tannin, so a grippy red that feels harsh on its own becomes smooth with steak or lamb.
examples: Avoid: big tannic reds with delicate fish

sections.term: Sweet wine should be sweeter than the dessert
sections.plain: Otherwise the wine tastes sour
sections.detail: Next to sweet food, a dry wine tastes thin and sharp. Choose a dessert wine at least as sweet as the pudding, and match weight to weight.
examples: Tawny Port with chocolate or nuts

questions.q: Why does a high-acid wine suit rich, fatty food?
opts: It refreshes your mouth between bites
questions.fact: Acidity cuts through fat like a squeeze of lemon.

questions.q: A tannic red tastes smoother with…
questions.fact: Protein and fat bind with tannin and soften it.

questions.q: With dessert, the wine should be…
opts: At least as sweet as the food
questions.fact: A drier wine tastes thin and sour next to sweet food.

tryIt.label: Scan a bottle for tonight's dinner

guides.title: Pairing with the food you actually eat
guides.subtitle: Pizza, curry, takeaway and Sunday roast: what to open with each.

sections.plain: Low alcohol, a little sweetness, no big tannin
sections.detail: Chilli heat makes alcohol and tannin feel hotter and harsher. Off-dry whites and juicy, low-tannin reds calm it down.
examples: Thai or Indian curry: off-dry Riesling or Gewürztraminer
Chilli con carne: Zinfandel or a juicy Grenache

sections.plain: Tomato wants acidity
sections.detail: Tomato is acidic, so it makes soft wines taste flat. Italian reds with fresh acidity are made for it.

sections.plain: Match the weight of the meat
sections.detail: Lighter meat, lighter wine. Smoky, charred food likes ripe, fruity reds.
examples: Roast chicken: Pinot Noir or oaked Chardonnay

questions.q: With a spicy curry, choose…
questions.fact: Heat amplifies alcohol and tannin; a touch of sweetness calms it.

questions.q: Tomato-based dishes suit wines with…
questions.fact: Tomato's acidity makes low-acid wines taste flat.

questions.q: Roast chicken pairs well with…
questions.fact: Lighter meats suit lighter, silkier reds or richer whites.

tryIt.label: Scan a bottle for tonight's dinner

guides.title: Wine and cheese without the guesswork
guides.subtitle: Why whites often beat reds with cheese, and three pairings that always work.

sections.plain: Tannin and cheese can clash
sections.detail: Many cheeses make tannic reds taste metallic or bitter. Fresh whites and sweet wines are the safer bet across a cheeseboard.
examples: Brie and Camembert: Champagne or Chardonnay
Hard cheeses: this is where reds work

sections.plain: Blue cheese loves sweet wine
sections.detail: Salt and sweetness balance each other, which is why blue cheese with a sweet wine is a classic.

sections.plain: Aged, hard cheeses
sections.detail: Firm, nutty cheeses stand up to reds, especially the grape's own region's cheese.
examples: Aged Comté with Jura or Burgundy

questions.q: Blue cheese is classically paired with…
opts: A sweet wine like Port or Sauternes
questions.fact: Salt and sweetness balance each other.

questions.q: Tannic reds often clash with…
questions.fact: Soft cheeses can make tannic reds taste metallic.

questions.q: A regional classic pairing is…
questions.fact: Food and wine from the same place grew up together.

guides.title: How much wine for a party
guides.subtitle: The numbers, the mix of styles, and what to have in reserve.

sections.plain: A bottle is five to six glasses
sections.detail: Plan on roughly half a bottle per guest for a dinner, a little more for a long party. It's easier to have a spare than run out.
examples: 20 guests at a party: about 12–15 bottles
Toast only: one bottle of sparkling fills 6–8 flutes

sections.plain: Match the season and the food
sections.detail: A rough split for mixed crowds is equal parts white and red, plus sparkling to start. Lean white and rosé in summer, red in winter.
examples: Summer: more white, rosé and sparkling

sections.plain: Plan the cold
sections.detail: Whites, rosés and sparkling need a few hours in the fridge, or 20 minutes in a bucket of ice and water. Light reds are better slightly cool too.
examples: Ice and water chills faster than ice alone
Light reds: 20 minutes in the fridge

questions.q: How many standard glasses in a 75cl bottle?
questions.fact: A standard 125–150ml pour gives five to six glasses.

questions.q: The fastest way to chill a bottle is…
opts: A bucket of ice and water
questions.fact: Water around the ice touches the whole bottle and chills it fast.

questions.q: For a summer party, lean towards…
questions.fact: Lighter, chilled styles suit warm weather.

guides.title: Serving order, temperature and leftovers
guides.subtitle: The small things that make a bottle taste its best, and keep it good tomorrow.

sections.plain: Light to heavy, dry to sweet
sections.detail: Serve lighter wines before fuller ones and dry before sweet, so each one doesn't make the next taste thin.

sections.plain: Whites are often too cold, reds too warm
sections.detail: Straight from the fridge mutes a good white; a warm room makes reds taste boozy. Take whites out ten minutes before serving and give reds ten minutes in the fridge.

sections.plain: Cork it and refrigerate it, even red
sections.detail: Oxygen and warmth are what spoil an open bottle. Recork it and keep it in the fridge; take a red out an hour before drinking.

questions.q: Serve wines in which order?
opts: Light to heavy, dry to sweet
questions.fact: Each wine then tastes as it should, not thin after a bigger one.

questions.q: Reds are best served at about…
questions.fact: Warm rooms make reds taste hot and boozy.

questions.q: An open bottle of red keeps best…
questions.fact: Cold slows oxidation, whatever the colour.

guides.title: Decanting: when it's worth it
guides.subtitle: Two reasons to decant, and the many wines that don't need it.

sections.plain: Old reds and vintage Port
sections.detail: Older reds and vintage Port throw a gritty deposit. Stand the bottle upright for a day, then pour slowly into a decanter, stopping when the sediment reaches the neck.
examples: Young wines: no sediment to remove

sections.term: To open up a young wine
sections.plain: Air softens young, tannic reds
sections.detail: An hour in a decanter can soften a young, grippy red and bring out its aromas.
examples: Young Pinot Noir: a short time at most
Delicate old wines: pour and drink

sections.plain: Most everyday wines don't need it
sections.detail: Fresh whites, rosés, sparkling and light reds are made to drink straight from the bottle.
examples: Swirling in the glass does much the same for a single glass

questions.q: One reason to decant an old red is to…
opts: Add oxygen to stop it ageing
questions.fact: Old reds throw a gritty deposit that decanting leaves behind.

questions.q: Which wine benefits most from an hour in a decanter?
questions.fact: Air softens young, grippy reds.

questions.q: Should you decant sparkling wine?
questions.fact: Decanting drives off the bubbles.
